newsitem.title: USA: U.S. faults Canada for salmon impasse.
newsitem.headline: U.S. faults Canada for salmon impasse.

text.p: The United States faulted Canada on Thursday for the failure to resolve a Pacific salmon dispute before the start of the 1997 fishing season.

Without a deal this summer, managers will ensure that U.S. fishing off the West Coast complies with "sound conservation and management principles and will coordinate with Canadian managers to that end," the State Department said.

In the latest round of failed talks, the United States put forward a package of proposals that would involve "major financial and social costs to U.S. interests," a statement said. It said they included a regime to rebuild depleted coho salmon stocks and a "significant" restructuring of the U.S. fishing fleet to reduce its catch of Fraser River sockeye.
In addition, the United States discussed establishment of a fund to conserve salmon stocks off the West Coast.

"Canada, however, was unwilling to make or accept a proposal that would meet the minimum necessary to assure conservation of Canadian and U.S. wild coho stocks, let alone allow both countries to maintain viable coho fisheries," the State Department said.

"In the end, Canada wanted the United States to make a substantial reduction in its sockeye fishery in return for a coho regime that would not ensure conservation and would not provide a coho fishery for the United States," it added.

In Canada, Foreign Affairs Minister Lloyd Axworthy said Canada was putting an end to months of talks over the issue and would set its own quotas. He said he wanted the United States to settle the dispute through binding arbitration.

Canada and the United States have been holding sporadic talks for the past few months on how to divide the Pacfic salmon catch. Both sides had hoped to reach an agreement before the salmon season started.

Talks initially broke down in May after Canada accused the United States of bargaining in bad faith. The governments of Canada and British Columbia threatened reprisals to pressure the United States into establishing fishing quotas.

Canada announced last month it would begin enforcing requirements for U.S. boats fishing in Canadian waters to report to Canadian authorities. Under that policy, the Canadian Coast Guard temporarily seized four U.S. fishing boats.

In its statement, the United States said it continued to favour so-called stakeholder talks as the best way for the two governments to reach agreement. The stakeholder process was established in February to let those whose interests were at the heart of the dispute try to find creative solutions.
